profile.campus: Chandler, Maricopa County, Arizona (CyrusOne Phoenix-metro campus, PHX1-PHX8)
profile.address: 2305 South Ellis Street, Building 5, Chandler, AZ 85286
profile.reading:
Per CyrusOne's own facility materials and an aggregator listing dedicated to this specific building, PHX3 sits at 2305 South Ellis Street, Building 5, Chandler, AZ 85286, part of CyrusOne's roughly 2,000,000 sq ft, eight-building Chandler campus (PHX1 through PHX8) totaling a publicly stated 169 MW of IT capacity across the whole campus; that campus-wide MW figure is not confirmed as this individual building's own capacity, so it is not asserted here as a single-building number.

Wikipedia's entry on CyrusOne states the company acquired 55.9 acres in Chandler in September 2011 for data center construction, part of its early-2010s national expansion under then-parent Cincinnati Bell before CyrusOne's own 2013 IPO; the company was founded in July 2000 by David Ferdman and Larry Bursten, headquartered in Dallas, Texas, and was taken private in a roughly $15 billion deal when Kohlberg Kravis Roberts (KKR) and Global Infrastructure Partners (GIP) acquired it, closing in March 2022. Chandler's electric and water utility, Salt River Project (SRP), serves this part of the Phoenix metro; Arizona data centers' water-intensive cooling systems have drawn scrutiny from local outlets including the Phoenix New Times given the state's arid climate and ongoing water-supply debates, a regional context relevant to this campus though not a site-specific consumption figure confirmed for this particular building.

Chandler's broader appeal to data center operators, alongside CyrusOne, the same submarket has drawn large campuses from other hyperscale and colocation players, stems from Arizona's relatively low natural-disaster risk profile (limited seismic activity, no hurricane exposure), business-friendly tax treatment for data center equipment under state statute, and proximity to fiber routes linking Phoenix to Los Angeles and other West Coast interconnection points, factors industry trade press has repeatedly cited in explaining the Phoenix metro's growth as a secondary US data center hub behind Northern Virginia and Texas.

reading.body:
CyrusOne PHX3 is one building in an eight-building Chandler campus (PHX1–PHX8) totaling roughly 2 million square feet and 169 MW of published IT capacity, though the individual building's own capacity is not confirmed. The Chandler campus sits in Arizona's Phoenix metropolitan region, which hosts 56 mapped data center facilities across the state, of which only four publish capacity figures; the eight-building PHX1–PHX8 complex ranks fifth by published megawatts in Arizona and represents roughly one-third of the state's 512 MW of publicly disclosed capacity. At typical AI training density of 40 kW per rack, the 169 MW campus-wide figure would correspond to approximately 4,200 racks as a single estimate, though this assumes all capacity runs at that intensity and applies the whole campus figure to validate the math.

The facility holds TIA-942 Class 4 certification, which qualifies it for mission-critical infrastructure loads including large compute clusters, and select buildings in the campus carry Energy Star Data Center Certification. These certifications speak to uptime and efficiency standards but do not specify which tenants occupy the space. The site is served by Salt River Project (SRP), the region's electric and water utility, and sits within Arizona's business-friendly tax framework for data center equipment; however, the campus's individual power draw, cooling water consumption, and grid interconnection capacity are not published.

Phoenix's appeal as a data center hub stems from low natural-disaster risk, favorable state tax treatment, and proximity to fiber routes linking the West Coast, factors that have drawn multiple large operators to the metro beyond CyrusOne. Arizona's water-intensive cooling demands have drawn regional scrutiny given the state's arid climate and water-supply constraints, a context relevant to any large campus here, though site-specific consumption for this building is not available. The Chandler campus was developed starting in 2011 on 55.9 acres; whether this facility currently hosts AI workloads, what fraction of its capacity is leased, or how much power it draws from the grid today is not published.
